articles.title: Russian court jails rights lawyer for 12 years on treason charge
articles.summary: Prosecutors say the woman shared security details with Ukraine, while her lawyers argue the information was not secret.
articles.body:
A court in Russia’s Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad has sentenced a 66-year-old rights lawyer to 12 years in prison for treason, after prosecutors accused her of passing sensitive information to Ukraine.

The court imposed the sentence on Thursday on Maria Bontsler, according to the rights group Slovo Zashchite, which said she had worked with a number of defendants accused of political offences in Kaliningrad.

The territory sits on the Baltic Sea between Lithuania and Poland.

A court statement posted on Telegram did not name her, but said she had been detained by the FSB intelligence agency on allegations of passing information to Ukraine beginning in 2024 about security officers in Kaliningrad.

Prosecutors also alleged she gave Ukraine information on criminal cases in the exclave that were of interest to Kyiv, the statement said.

She was also given an extra year of restrictions on her activity. Prosecutors had sought 15 years, according to Slovo Zashchite.

Slovo Zashchite said the trial was held behind closed doors, with Bontsler and her lawyers prevented from attending, and that she was allowed only to make a closing statement. It said her lawyers argued that none of the information cited by prosecutors was secret, and that she had been in ill health in detention.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, parliament has approved laws that make public actions aimed at “discrediting” the army illegal and ban the spread of “fake news” about the armed forces.

Russian courts have also jailed lawyers who took on politically sensitive cases. In January 2025, a court sentenced three lawyers of the late opposition leader Alexey Navalny to between three and a half and five and a half years on “extremism” charges, in a case widely seen as an effort to discourage defence lawyers from taking political cases.

articles.title: London financier spent over 20 years living in his mother's £3.85 million Chelsea home before demanding a £2.6 million share; judge rejected his claim and ordered him to pay £85,000 annually
articles.summary: Living in a family-owned property for decades does not necessarily give someone a legal claim to ownership, even when there have been discussions about
articles.body: Living in a family-owned property for decades does not necessarily give someone a legal claim to ownership, even when there have been discussions about inheritance. That distinction became central to a dispute involving London financier Andrew Grijns and his 80-year-old mother, Janice Grijns, over a four-bedroom townhouse in Chelsea. Andrew had lived in the property for more than 20 years, but after his father's death, the relationship between mother and son deteriorated. He eventually went to court seeking two-thirds of the house's value, around £2.6 million, as reported by The Independent. The High Court rejected his claim, declared him a trespasser and ordered him to pay £85,000 for every year he remained after August 2023.The £3.85 million Chelsea townhouse Andrew lived in for more than 20 yearsThe property at the centre of the dispute is a four-storey Georgian terraced house in Bury Walk, Chelsea. Reportedly, Andrew's parents, Janice and Leendert Grijns, bought the property in 1994. The Chelsea townhouse was valued at approximately £3.85 million in July 2024. The building has four bedrooms and a separate basement flat, providing accommodation as well as a base for the family when they spent time in London.Leendert worked in banking, while Janice had a background in real estate before moving into academia. Their son was also building a career in London's financial sector, which was one of the reasons behind the purchase. The family wanted a place where he could stay while working in the capital, but the house also served as a holiday property for his parents.Janice used the London base to enjoy the city's theatres, opera and restaurants, as well as to pursue her interest in antiques. Andrew moved into the townhouse around 1999 and continued living there for much of his adult life.The arrangement lasted more than two decades. During that period, he was able to maintain a home in one of London's expensive neighbourhoods without purchasing a separate property of his own.How an inheritance discussion became a £2.6 million claimThe disagreement was rooted partly in conversations about what would happen to the Chelsea property after the parents' deaths. Andrew had asked for a larger share of the London house than his three brothers, citing possible complications involving US tax authorities if he inherited American assets following his mother's death.In 2015, Janice sent him an email setting out her intention to leave him two-thirds of the property's value, with the remaining third divided between his brothers. Andrew responded by describing himself as lucky and grateful.That correspondence later became important to his legal argument. He maintained that his parents had given him assurances about the future of the property and that he had made decisions about his life on the understanding that he would eventually receive a substantial share.His claim was based on the legal doctrine of proprietary estoppel. Andrew argued that he had organised his life around promises made by his parents from around 2004. He said he had stayed in the family home, carried out improvements and passed up opportunities to purchase somewhere independently because he believed he would eventually receive two-thirds of the Chelsea property.He also argued that remaining in the house had involved sacrifices. According to his case, the building was larger than he needed, its traditional interiors were not to his taste and maintaining it was expensive. He claimed he would otherwise have preferred to establish a home of his own.The relationship deteriorated after his father's deathThe family relationship had reportedly been close before the dispute began. Things changed after Leendert died in 2019, leaving Janice as the sole owner of the Chelsea property.Andrew was also going through a divorce and had become involved in a legal disagreement with a former friend. Tensions between him and his mother increased, with both making serious accusations during their exchanges.In June 2020, the pair exchanged heated emails. Andrew accused Janice of bullying him, turning against him and attempting to damage his reputation. His mother, in turn, accused him of wanting her dead so that he could obtain the house.Janice eventually made her position clear, telling her son that he should leave the property as soon as possible. She did not believe they could continue living under the same roof while he was speaking about her in such terms.Judge rejects son's claim and criticises his conduct towards his elderly motherThe case was heard at the High Court, where Master Timothy Bowles examined Andrew's claims and the documentary evidence presented during the proceedings. The judge was not persuaded that Andrew had remained in the property because of promises about future ownership. He considered that the arrangement had suited Andrew, allowing him to live in a substantial Chelsea home at relatively little expense while pursuing a well-paid career in finance.Bowles also questioned why Andrew would have chosen to remain in a property that he described as too large, expensive to maintain and unsuitable for his preferences if he had genuinely been making significant sacrifices in reliance on his parents' assurances.The judge took issue with Andrew's failure to recognise the advantages he had received from his parents over the years. His assessment of the financier was particularly critical, describing him as self-absorbed and saying that his main concern appeared to be his own interests.The ruling rejected the suggestion that Andrew had shaped his adult life because of binding assurances from his parents. The judge concluded that personal convenience, rather than an expectation of inheriting the property, explained why he had stayed.He also criticised Andrew's conduct during the proceedings, including the pressure placed on his elderly mother through litigation. The case had involved questions about Janice's mental capacity, alongside a later attempt by Andrew to have her committed to prison over her efforts to regain possession of the house.£85,000 for every year he stayed after August 2023The financial consequences of the judgment extended beyond the dismissal of the £2.6 million claim. The judge declared Andrew to have been trespassing at the property from August 1, 2023, after his mother had demanded that he leave.The judge ordered Andrew to pay mesne profits at an annual rate of £85,000 from August 1, 2023, until he handed back possession. The amount was based on the rental value of the entire property, including the separate basement flat, and was intended to compensate his mother for his continued occupation after he had become a trespasser.Andrew must also account for rental income he received from letting part of the property from May 2023. The court's order therefore covered not only his continued residence but also money generated through the property's use during the disputed period.The legal costs added another substantial burden. The bill was expected to exceed £1 million, with Janice's legal expenses alone estimated at approximately £750,000. Andrew would also have to meet his own legal costs. The financial outcome left him facing a considerable bill after losing his attempt to secure a two-thirds interest in the house.Disclaimer: This article is based on information publicly reported. The Times of India has not independently verified the property valuation, financial claims or circumstances of the family dispute. The legal findings and court orders are reported as stated in the judgment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A French homeowner digging a swimming pool in his backyard uncovered 5 gold bars and hundreds of coins worth €700,000; the previous owner's death has left the discovery unexplained
articles.summary: A homeowner in Neuville-sur-Saône, near Lyon in France, unearthed a fortune buried in his garden while preparing to install a swimming pool.
articles.body: A homeowner in Neuville-sur-Saône, near Lyon in France, unearthed a fortune buried in his garden while preparing to install a swimming pool. The discovery, made during excavation work in May 2025, included 5 gold bars and hundreds of gold coins packed inside plastic bags. The treasure was valued at approximately €700,000, turning an ordinary home improvement project into an extraordinary find. Although authorities confirmed that the gold could legally remain with the homeowner, the circumstances behind its burial have continued to raise questions, particularly because the property's previous owner had died.French homeowner discovered €700,000 worth of gold treasure in backyardAccording to French regional newspaper Le Progrès, the discovery happened at a property in Neuville-sur-Saône, a town located near Lyon. The homeowner had purchased the house approximately a year earlier and decided to undertake construction work to install a swimming pool in the garden.During the excavation, workers discovered several plastic bags buried in the ground. Inside them were 5 gold bars and numerous gold coins, carefully stored together beneath the garden's surface.Le Progrès said in November 2025 the treasure was estimated to be worth around €700,000. The homeowner, who has not been publicly identified, didn’t try to keep the find under wraps. Instead, he went directly to the local town hall to declare the treasure, setting in motion a process to determine whether he could legally retain it.How did authorities determine who could keep the goldThe discovery was reported to the relevant authorities, including the Regional Directorate of Cultural Affairs, known as DRAC in France. The organisation was involved in determining whether the buried objects had archaeological importance.As Le Progrès explained, the French state can intervene when a discovery is considered historically or archaeologically significant. In such circumstances, officials may order an expert assessment and potentially claim ownership of the objects. However, the gold uncovered in Neuville-sur-Saône did not meet that threshold.The Independent reported that local authorities had confirmed the homeowner was entitled to keep the treasure after officials established that it had no archaeological significance. The decision meant the discovery would not become a state-owned historical collection.Police traced the gold to a legitimate sourceThe discovery also prompted checks by law enforcement, as authorities needed to establish whether the gold had been connected to criminal activity.According to Le Progrès, the gendarmerie examined the five gold bars as part of its investigation. Each bar carried an identification number, making it possible to trace its origins and check whether it had been connected to a burglary or theft in the surrounding region.The investigation established that the gold had been acquired legally. The Brussels Times reported that the bars and coins had been melted by a company in the Lyon area approximately 15 to 20 years earlier.This detail helped to distinguish the find from possible stolen valuables or archeological discovery. The gold did not appear to be connected to any recent crime, but rather to have been lawfully acquired and then buried on the property.The checks also cleared the way for the homeowner to retain the valuable collection without facing a claim from the state.The previous owner's death leaves the treasure unexplainedDespite the investigation establishing the gold's legal origins, one important question remains unanswered: who buried the treasure in the garden, and why.Le Progrès reported that the property's previous owner was believed to have died. Nobody appeared to know who had hidden the gold or what circumstances had led to its burial.The homeowner had only acquired the property around a year before the discovery, according to Le Progrès. That meant the treasure had been buried before his ownership, although the precise date when it was placed there remains unclear.The gold's relatively recent origins, estimated at around 15 to 20 years, make the mystery particularly intriguing. Unlike ancient coins or historical artefacts, the collection appears to have been hidden during a period within living memory.With the gold valued at approximately €700,000 and the authorities confirming his right to retain it, the homeowner became the lawful possessor of a substantial fortune. articles.title: Microsoft Outlook and other services down; company says it's investigating
articles.summary: The outage was affecting numerous Microsoft services.
articles.body:
Microsoft said it was investigating an outage Thursday that left people unable to access Outlook email and other products.

In a message posted at 12:54 p.m. ET on the official Microsoft 365 Status account on X, the company said it was "investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas." In an update at 1:07 p.m. ET, the company said it had "confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region."

Outage tracking site Downdetector showed an increase in reports that hit a peak just before 1 p.m. ET. Thousands of users reported problems with its Outlook, Copilot, Teams and Sharepoint services, and some even reported problems accessing Microsoft Word and Excel.

Microsoft did not provide a cause for the outage, but said on X that it was offering updates in its admin center, which also appeared to be down Thursday afternoon. In its X posts, Microsoft said its systems were experiencing an "elevated load" and that it was "redistributing connection traffic" across its infrastructure.

As of 5 p.m. ET, Microsoft said the issue was still not resolved and that it was "opening all available pathways to restore service."

Microsoft suffered another widespread outage in September, when the Microsoft 365 suite, which includes Outlook, was down for several days.

articles.title: Federal Title IX probe rocks Camas School District after trans runner controversy, superintendent pushes back
articles.summary: Camas High's cross-country controversy deepens as the Department of Education opens a Title IX investigation into the district's handling of complaints.
articles.body: Think the controversy surrounding the male Camas High cross-country runner who switched to the girls' team ended when the season did? Not even close. OutKick has learned that the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights opened an investigation into Washington state's Camas School District today to determine whether it violated Title IX. A CROSS COUNTRY RUNNER SWITCHED TO THE GIRLS TEAM MIDSEASON, PARENTS VOICE THEIR DISAPPROVAL AT MEET As was first reported by 570-KVI, parents and members of the Camas High girls' cross-country team alleged last month that the male runner entered a hotel room occupied by three female runners and took an ice bath in their bathroom while the team was traveling for an invitational meet. There are also allegations that the athlete sexually harassed female teammates, raising concerns about their privacy and safety. Parents also accused the district of mishandling their complaints of sexual harassment. They alleged that an independent investigator failed to take steps to protect the girls and instead questioned whether they were "transphobic" or "hate trans people." This all comes on the heels of the Camas runner switching from the boys to the girls' team in the middle of the season, which ended Saturday in the state finals. The runner finished 76th in a JV meet in his first race as a boy, but won a varsity meet upon switching to the girls' team and prevented girls from advancing to the regional and state meets. The runner's presence on the girls' team sparked three separate protests from female athletes — including about a dozen of his own teammates — who walked off the starting line after the gun sounded rather than compete against him. Elise Bierer of Battle Ground High ended her season by walking off the starting line at the district meet. The consequences for Camas School District? They could be significant. According to the DOE, a Title IX violation can result in the loss of federal funding. But Camas School District Superintendent John Anzalone isn't particularly worried. 'HEARTBROKEN' WASHINGTON STATE SUPERINTENDENT SAYS NO CONSEQUENCES FOR GIRLS WHO PROTESTED TRANSGENDER RUNNER In an interview with OutKick on Thursday, Anzalone said he was confident the district had handled the controversy appropriately and didn't expect the federal investigation to uncover any violations. "I don't think there are going to be any violations," said Anzalone, emphasizing that he trusts that his staff acted appropriately throughout this ordeal. "And if there were, and we made a misstep somewhere, we'll move forward and correct that." This came after a back-and-forth regarding the ice baths, which Anzalone downplayed. Last month, Clark County Today quoted an anonymous Camas parent who said the following: "[Biological male’s name redacted] entered a hotel room shared by three girls to take an ice bath,’’ the parent said. "The ice bath is a CHS tradition, but it is, of course, against school policy for boys to enter girls' rooms and vice versa. Presumably, he stripped down to his shorts and sports bra like the girls do among themselves for the ice bath.’’ Anzalone, however, said the ice bath incident was "highly blown out of proportion" and that district administrators never felt anything inappropriate had occurred. He explained that the ice baths were a team tradition that district leadership hadn't been aware of. He also clarified that the male runner stayed in a separate hotel room with his mother, rather than sharing one with female teammates. I pushed back on Anzalone's characterization of the ice bath incident, pointing out that the tradition generally involves athletes of the same sex and that one girl reportedly felt uncomfortable enough to leave the room. Anzalone said his understanding was that the girl left as soon as the transgender runner entered. He also reiterated that the district couldn't prevent an activity it didn't know was happening. PARENTS SPEAK OUT ON THE INGRAHAM ANGLE AFTER GIRLS FORFEIT RACE OVER BIOLOGICAL MALE RUNNER But when I asked whether he understood why mixing genders in such a setting would concern parents and athletes, he acknowledged the point. "Yeah, absolutely, absolutely," Anzalone said. "I'm not denying that." He maintained, however, that his primary concern was ensuring such activities took place in an appropriate setting with adult supervision, regardless of gender. In fact, Anzalone acknowledged that the district has since changed its protocols to ensure administrators are aware of team traditions and that activities such as ice baths have adult supervision. The superintendent also said he wouldn't necessarily have supported ice baths in hotel rooms in the first place, regardless of the athletes' genders. But the ice bath controversy was hardly the only source of frustration for the girls on the team. When I asked Anzalone whether he would have handled anything differently, given the protests, the athletes who quit and the turmoil surrounding the program, he acknowledged that the district might have done more to make every student feel supported. He compared the situation to a parent with multiple children, one of whom is going through a particularly difficult time. "If you have multiple children and one is going through something really serious, you kind of feel like, oh man, am I neglecting the other kids?" Anzalone said. "We want to make sure that we're not doing that. And if we did make those missteps, I know that, at least at the school level, they're working to make sure they correct that." Anzalone described the situation as a "lose-lose," explaining that supporting one group of students could leave another feeling neglected. "Trying to find that happy medium," he said, "That's not easy to do." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Anzalone said the controversy has largely quieted down within Camas High School, adding that he hopes students can return to focusing on academics and athletics rather than the political debate surrounding the team. "It's still from day one, it breaks my heart that any of the students had to kind of take this activist role or decided to take that role," he said. The superintendent also said he would cooperate fully with the Department of Education's investigation and provide whatever documents federal officials request. "If there's more that comes out in this, that even I didn't know, then I'll be happy to either answer to it, be accountable to it or change course if necessary," Anzalone said. articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis renew strikes on Saudi Arabia as UNSC extends sanctions
articles.summary: Saudi-led coalition intercepts flurry of suspected Houthi drones targeting oil and military infrastructure.
articles.body:
Saudi-led coalition forces have said they intercepted suspected Houthi drones over Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh region and Eastern Province, as the UN Security Council agreed to extend sanctions on the Iran-allied group.

Major General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, announced the interceptions of suspected Houthi drones on Thursday, in a statement carried by the Saudi Press Agency.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had targeted oil infrastructure and military assets in the kingdom, including a pumping station on the East-West Pipeline with a drone as well as the Yanbu oil facility on the Red Sea.

Riyadh says it has rerouted about 4 million barrels of crude per day via its East-West Pipeline to Yanbu, equivalent to about 4 percent of global supply.

Saree further claimed a military cargo plane at Sharurah airport close to Yemen’s border was targeted with a drone, while a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait airbase “scored a direct hit”.

The Houthi spokesperson added that their forces had targeted the Saudi Aramco headquarters in the capital, Riyadh, but rejected as a “grave falsehood” a Saudi assertion that the group had targeted the kingdom’s Mecca region on Wednesday.

Saudi-backed coalition forces fighting on behalf of Yemen’s internationally recognised government say they continue to confront the Houthis across all frontlines, targeting leaders, vehicles, reinforcements, weapons and positions.

Yemen’s Defence Ministry, citing the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, said the battle against the Houthis was moving towards its “desired objectives”, according to Yemen’s official pro-government Saba news agency.

A meeting convened by the Defence Ministry was held in the Marib governorate to discuss the ongoing operations against the Houthis, where ways to enhance coordination and integration between various military units that are part of the Dawn of Yemen offensive were also discussed.

On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) unanimously voted in favour of extending sanctions related to Yemen for one more year, including freezing assets and enforcing travel bans, while demanding an end to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The mandate for the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, which made the recommendations, was also extended.

UNSC members called on “all parties to refrain from escalatory actions and to resolve differences and disputes through negotiation”, while also backing the territorial integrity of both Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

“The resolution condemns the military escalation by the Houthis, their maritime and cross-border attacks against Saudi Arabia, and their threats to commercial shipping vessels,” the UNSC statement said.

The resolution emphasised that measures taken for the purpose of maintaining sanctions “shall not apply to humanitarian assistance or supplies for basic needs of civilians, without negatively affecting legitimate trade activities”.

“The council sanctions are merely a means, not an end in themselves,” said Ambassador Fu Cong, China’s envoy to the UN, who hoped that “the situation in Yemen will de-escalate as soon as possible”.

On Thursday, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said more than 333,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since the beginning of August, including more than 24,000 displaced in the past week.

Civilians “continue to pay a heavy price as violence damages health facilities, forces families from their homes, and hinders the work of humanitarians”, OCHA said.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is pressing the European Union to adopt an EU Parliament resolution to designate the Ansar Allah Houthi movement as a “terrorist organisation”, according to the Reuters news agency, citing sources familiar with the drive.

But European officials told Reuters the bloc is concerned this could undermine a future peace process.

EU foreign policy spokesperson Anouar El-Anouni said the bloc was in regular contact with Riyadh on regional developments, but declined to comment on any specific discussions under way, according to Reuters.

I've been in there with Slade, I've felt him when he has the advantage of numbers, and now, if it's just me and him, I've got things to get out of my system, and for him to return to wrestling and for him to knowingly know, the last time or one of the times he wrestled me, he disappeared from this business for two years, they can say what they want about, ‘Oh, is Effy scared of Slade?’ But historically, I have made or break careers along the way." It’s tough talk but that’s who Effy is. He’s one of the top independent pro wrestlers on the scene today as he was ranked No. 72 on Pro Wrestling Illustrated’s Top 500 for 2026. articles.title: Skye Newman gets 'goosebumps' over record-breaking Brixton Academy run
articles.summary: She is the first British female solo singer to play a five-gig residency at the venue.
articles.body:
Fast rising pop star Skye Newman began her November five-gig run at Brixton Academy on Thursday - a record for a British female solo artist

The BBC Sound of 2026 winner is set to overtake rapper Little Simz, who headlined three nights at the legendary south London venue in 2021.

It will cap an incredible few years for Brit Award nominee Newman, 23, who performed at Radio 1's Big Weekend in Sunderland last month.

Speaking to BBC News's Mark Savage ahead of her record-breaking run, Newman said it had given her "goosebumps and chills". She added: "It's crazy. My jaw drops all the time. I feel honoured to be the first woman, and I don't take it lightly."

Born in south-east London, the "loud, raw and strikingly honest" Newman - according to our music correspondent - exploded onto the scene last year when her debut single, Hairdresser, went straight into the top 20.

The follow-up, Family Matters, reached number five in June. It was the first time a female artist had made the top 20 with their first two singles since Ella Henderson in 2014.

The husky-voiced soul and R&B singer has previously supported Ed Sheeran and Lewis Capaldi on tour, and been called "incredibly talented" and "something else" by Sir Elton John.

Now she stands on the shoulders of pop giants.

Historically, US pop-punk icon Debby Harry and Romy Croft, frontwoman of the band The XX have also enjoyed big Brixton residencies, as well as Phoebe Bridgers, Chappell Roan and Tash Sultana.

But after three more gigs this weekend and one added one next, Newman will newly lead the way for UK female solo stars at one of the country's most prestigious venues.

She also insists on having an all-female band on stage with her.

"Women are the centre of my world," she said. "They're the people that built me. They allowed me space to grow and find myself. So, I definitely had to take that out on stage with me.

"I had to stand by what I stand by. It's quite scary at the minute how much social media is [affecting how women are being treated] so I'm just really big on trying to keep women everywhere."

She continued: "If I can have a woman in place, I will. I'll give a job out. I'll give my helping hand always."

Newman recently paid tribute to another soulful London singer to have graced the same space back in 2007, the late Amy Winehouse, with a rendition of her song Addicted during a special Back to Black anniversary gig for the BBC.

"The thing with Amy's music is it's so incredible that you don't want to touch it," she admitted.

"No-one would ever do it like Amy, and I think it was definitely scary for all of us... that feeling of, you've got to live up to that expectation. You've got to fill her shoes, and they're big shoes to fill.

"But I think we all smashed it, and I think it was honestly the most beautiful, inspirational day I've had in a very long time."

Next month she will head off to Australia with Harry Styles for a series of support slots, which the childhood One Direction fan says is "surreal", and something she agreed to with "no questions asked".

"'Whatever I've got, cancel it'," she joked she had told her team on hearing about the request.

"It felt like a dream because I was the age of One Direction [fans], so that was around when I was a child and obviously I loved them and Harry and Zane were my favourites.

"So then now to go and support Harry Styles is just mental."

articles.title: Super Bowl champion Kyle Van Noy details what really happens when a player gets traded at the deadline
articles.summary: Super Bowl champion Kyle Van Noy revealed the behind-the-scenes chaos of his 2016 trade from the Detroit Lions to the New England Patriots.
articles.body: Ever wonder what it’s like to be traded in the NFL midseason? Well, if you have, you are in luck. Super Bowl champion Kyle Van Noy, who currently plays for the Minnesota Vikings, took to social media to share his experience of being traded at the deadline. The 35-year-old was traded from the Detroit Lions to the New England Patriots in 2016. "I got a call from the Lions GM at the time saying I was traded (he forgot to tell me until the end of the call where I was traded to). You then get a call from the team that traded for you (patriots). They set a flight up with you as fast as possible," Van Noy said on X. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE He explained that the team that acquires a player wants to bring him in as fast as possible to complete a physical. Van Noy said teams want to avoid a situation like the one involving Maxx Crosby during the offseason, when the Baltimore Ravens backed out of a trade days after agreeing to it with the Las Vegas Raiders because of concerns about his physical. Van Noy said teams will help players with some moving and living arrangements after a trade. "The only thing when I was traded the team took care of was moving. Teams give you a certain amount of money for movers and shipping your car. Lastly, team takes care of about 10 days or 2 weeks paid for a hotel room until you can find your own living," Van Noy said. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! However, when it comes to a player's previous residence, they are responsible for handling those arrangements themselves. "You can sell the house with a realtor if you bought one in the city you play in or renting you gotta pay the rest of the rent even if you are not living in it," Van Noy said. Van Noy hasn't been traded midseason since 2016 and said things could have changed since then, but he believes the process remains largely the same. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD Van Noy is in his 13th NFL season and his first with the Vikings. He has played for six different teams during his career. He spent the first two and a half seasons of his career with the Lions before being traded to the Patriots, where he spent three and a half seasons. He was with the Miami Dolphins for one season before returning to the Patriots. Van Noy then signed with the Los Angeles Chargers, where he spent one season before playing the following three seasons with the Baltimore Ravens. In his first season with the Vikings, he has recorded 15 total tackles and 1.5 sacks in eight games.

articles.title: The school where white working-class pupils defy the odds
articles.summary: Politicians are worried about the outcomes of white, working-class pupils. But one school in Sunderland seems to have defied gravity
articles.body:
Two years ago, I stood in a school hall in Sunderland on GCSE results day and watched the pride and surprise in the faces of teenagers as the envelopes were opened.

Even after years of covering results days, I was emotional to see a set of outstanding results in a school facing so many challenges. Almost half of the school's pupils receive free school meals, meaning their parents are on low incomes. In fact, the results in the ex-mining town of Hetton-le-Hole were as strong as the most affluent parts of southern England.

This summer, Hetton Academy hit another milestone, with 80% of its pupils getting a pass of at least a grade 4 in maths and English. A grade 4 is roughly equivalent to a 'C' under the old system, and is seen as a passport to jobs and further education.

Another striking detail about Hetton is that almost all of its pupils are from a white, working-class background, a group that's been in the spotlight for some time. This week saw the launch of the second phase of an independent inquiry, led by former Cabinet minister Baroness Morris, into why children from those communities lag behind their peers at school. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: "Right now, too many white, working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education."

But Hetton Academy seems to have defied the odds. The school's principal, Vicky Pinkney, refuses to accept low incomes should mean low results. "I don't think we should be accepting less just because of the community you work in," she says.

The stellar results have won Hetton a place among an elite group of schools: mainstream secondaries that don't select pupils academically, and where 80% of pupils get that all-important grade 4 in maths and English.

In fact, there were only 339 non-selective schools in England that hit an average 80% pass rate in maths and English for the three years to 2025, out of around 3,000 that published the relevant data. High achieving schools have been the focus of some political attention recently, with MPs in several parties arguing that we should study them closely.

What can they tell us about how to raise standards? And could other schools facing the same challenges as Hetton achieve equally impressive results?

From a quick glance of those 339 high-achieving schools, it becomes clear that some of their success comes from things that are difficult to shift.

In particular, the economic profile of the pupils clearly matters. Schools that hit the average 80% pass rate have fewer children from the lowest-income families than average, and are less likely to be in deprived areas. They also have fewer children with special educational needs.

Analysts say we shouldn't be surprised by the huge role played by family finances in determining a school's outcome.

Prof John Jerrim, an academic at University College London who researches education systems in different countries, says that England's system is failing poorer pupils.

Since 2010, even while an overhaul of GCSEs has been widely seen as raising standards, the likelihood of the children from the poorest families passing these key exams has barely changed, he says.

"It's really hard to move the dial," says Prof Jerrim.

Seamus Murphy, CEO of Turner Schools, which runs schools in financially deprived areas, thinks the push for higher academic standards under Michael Gove from 2010 instilled "vision and challenge" into the system. But it doesn't work for all pupils, he says.

Especially in places where families are struggling with the cost of living, he says, an 18-year-old earning the minimum wage was "a big deal", and it might be tempting for some parents to push their children towards work rather than education.

The high-performing schools on our list also have a lower proportion of pupils from a White British background than other schools. Earlier this year, Baroness Morris's inquiry found that many white, working-class families have simply lost faith in the school system and increasingly believe it does not guarantee future success.

Morning quizzes and fish and chips evenings

So it's clear that a school's fortunes are shaped in part by factors outside its control.

But there's a complication. When you zoom in on particular schools, some of them do seem to be able to defy gravity, achieving high results despite seemingly being on the 'wrong' side of those demographic factors.

So back to that school in Sunderland. It stands out as something of an exception: it has a mostly white, working-class population, and lots of pupils from poor families. In fact, if you just look at the very highest grades, the region in which Hetton sits came bottom of the English league table this year. Just 3% of GCSEs in the North East were given the top mark (a grade 9) this summer, versus 8% in London, according to exam watchdog Ofqual. (On other measures of GCSE performance, the North East ranked more favourably.)

After opening in the 1960s under the name Hetton School, it struggled for years with low performance. Hetton-le-Hole town was hit hard by the closure of the Eppleton mine in the 1980s. It became common for families to send their children elsewhere in search of a good education. An Ofsted report in 2021 ranked the school as "requires improvement". That was the last report before it converted into an academy.

But by 2024, Ofsted said it was "rapidly improving". This year's 80% pass rate for maths and English GCSEs ranks the school high within the Sunderland local authority, and well above the average for England, where 57% passed maths and 60% passed English.

It's now the "school of choice" for local families, says the principal, Pinkney.

The school also says it aims to have a warm, welcoming ethos.

For Year 11 pupils, there is a separate entrance path which is lined each morning by teachers who stop a few and quiz them about their subject, problem solving on the spot with a whiteboard.

While it's done in a good-humoured way, the decision on who to stop for this brief intervention is discussed at regular review meetings.

There is more structured support for everyone in the form of an hour of extra study four days a week after school. If maths is where you are stuck, you might do two of these hours on that subject.

Over the run-up to exams, the school holds 'Revision Sundays', when the Year 11 pupils can come in for a top-up session and eat a roast lunch together.

It's all designed to foster a feeling of inclusion in the classroom, which in turn can boost exam grades, the school thinks. And it seems to be working. When reviewing the school in 2024, Ofsted praised the "positive relationships" enjoyed between pupils and staff.

And a government-commissioned study, published this year by the University of Cambridge, found that pupils who say they "belong" in school see "significantly higher attainment" in their GCSEs.

Around this time of year at Hetton, parents of Year 11 pupils, who will sit exams next summer, receive an invitation to a 'Fish and Tips' evening at the school. They'll get advice on what they can do as parents to support learning and a bag full of revision resources. Booklets and stationery are tailored to each pupil.

Afterwards Pinkney and the other staff sit down with them for fish and chips in the canteen, paid for by the school. The parents see her as "just another Mam", she says, who wants their children to do their best. She says some of the parents may have had a poor experience of school, or simply been able to get into work without many qualifications themselves.

It's a community that mostly "stays in the area", Pinkney says, and it's the school's task to "open their horizons".

But still, challenges remain. It certainly won't be easy for every school in a white, working-class area to emulate Hetton's success.

Prof Lindsey Macmillan, an expert in how education shapes life chances, was involved in the recent inquiry into white working-class children.

The pupils start school already behind, she says, and that gap only widens through secondary school due to a growing disengagement with education.

The inquiry found "telling" evidence that the connection with school "falls off a cliff" for white working-class families at the point of moving to secondary school, leading to poor attendance.

Parents told the inquiry things like, "I didn't need qualifications" to get into work - the same message as Pinkney hears from some parents in Hetton-le-Hole. (In reality, Macmillan says, formal qualifications are now more important for getting a job than they were in previous decades, when there were more routes into well-paid industrial work, and more on-the-job training.)

That's a point supported by Prof Jerrim, who thinks schools should get families to buy-in on education by clearly explaining to them how qualifications can help their children find work.

The inquiry also reported a sense of white working-class parents not wanting their children to leave their area, with its strong sense of connection. England's education system was described as being out-of-step with the values of white, working-class communities. Parents in those areas are ambitious for their children, the inquiry found, but often prioritise happiness and life-readiness alongside or above high grades.

But Macmillan, an education professor at University College London, also says that high grades shouldn't be seen as the only route into successful adult life. To suggest that sounds "demeaning" to some parents who didn't achieve high grades themselves, she thinks.

"Why have we created a structure where getting those maths and English GCSEs is so important to your life chances?" she says.

She wants the government to think about more entry-level apprenticeships and other on-the-job learning, so children with lower academic grades can still thrive.

Back in Sunderland, the 700 or so pupils at Hetton Academy have just arrived back in school after their half-term.

Does the principal think other places could replicate its success?

Absolutely, Pinkney says. And for her, it's personal: she points out that she too was raised by a single mother with little money, and still thrived academically.

"I feel really strongly about that. My school helped me to be able to achieve."

articles.title: Timothée Chalamet among Hollywood stars and charity heroes stepping up for BBC Children In Need
articles.summary: Viewers of the annual TV charity event will see the actor playing a prank on Rylan.
articles.body:
This year's BBC Children In Need show is taking place on Friday, with highlights including Timothee Chalamet pranking Rylan Clark, and a "challenge squad" of young people completing feats in the name of charity.

Oscar-nominated actor Chalamet and co-stars Zendaya, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy will be seen making Rylan sweat during an interview for their new film Dune: Part Three, with the help of three children, hidden behind the scenes.

The show will also feature Radio 2 presenter Owain Wyn Evans, on a 400-mile cycle challenge through Scotland, Northern Ireland, England and Wales.

Last year's appeal raised more than £45m to help children and young people across the UK, and this year's TV event will be broadcast from 19:00 GMT.

The three-hour show will be hosted live from Salford by Alex Jones, Mel Giedroyc, Rylan, Sara Cox and Tyler West.

They will welcome Wyn Evans, who has been the latest Radio 2 DJ to put himself through a gruelling challenge for Children In Need, following in the footsteps of the likes of Sara Cox and Paddy McGuinness.

Wyn Evans is being joined on his final leg in Wales on Friday by 22-year-old Harri, who is living with hidden lasting effects of a brain tumour.

He is part of The One Show's "challenge squad" - four young people who have signed up for a series of personal missions for the charity.

The others are 16-year old Zoe, who has Down's syndrome, who will be seen dancing with the cast of High School Musical; Ana, also 16, who has a rare physical condition and is doing a three-day kayaking challenge; and 22-year-old Serena, who will perform live in memory of her late brother and a childhood friend.

The theme of this year's Children In Need is Challenge Yourself 2026, which has also seen Morning Live presenters Michelle Ackerley and Gethin Jones learn instruments to perform with a band live on the night.

Joe Wicks and Emma Bunton are among the other stars who have been involved, while landmarks including the Blackpool Tower, London Eye and Titanic Belfast will be lit in yellow for the occasion.

Children in Need supports more than 1,600 local charities and projects across the UK.

Children In Need is on BBC One and iPlayer from 19:00-22:00 GMT on Friday.
